summary: Describes a format for an LDAP Uniform Resource Locator, allowing Internet clients direct access to the LDAP directory protocol. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 2255.

plainLanguage.summary: An LDAP URL describes a directory lookup in a link: it can identify an LDAP server and entry, choose attributes, set a search scope, and provide a filter. RFC 1959 was later replaced by RFC 2255.

questions: how to write an ldap url
what are the parts of an ldap url
what happens when ldap url fields are omitted
subtitle: A URL format for requesting an LDAP directory lookup

tldr.problem: Clients needed a standard URL form that gives direct access to an LDAP query.
tldr.mechanism: An LDAP URL identifies a directory name and can specify returned attributes, search scope and filter, with defaults when parts are omitted.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1959 defined the proposed format and was later replaced by RFC 2255.

sections.title: A URL for an LDAP Query
sections.content:
LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. This RFC describes a Uniform Resource Locator format that lets Internet clients access LDAP directly. The format can refer to a server-backed directory and is general enough for a stand-alone LDAP server.

An LDAP URL begins with ldap:// and includes a distinguished name path. It may also include the server and port, requested attributes, search scope and a filter.
sections.plainLanguage: An LDAP URL describes what directory information a client should look up. It can name a server and specify which entry or entries to search.

sections.title: URL Parts and Search Defaults
sections.content:
The optional host and port identify an LDAP server; the default port is TCP 389. The distinguished name identifies an entry. The attributes part selects which attributes to return, and the scope can be base, one or sub. URL-illegal characters, such as spaces, are escaped using the percent method described in RFC 1738.

If attributes are omitted, all attributes are returned. If scope is omitted, the default is a base-object search. If the filter is omitted, the default filter is (objectClass=*). An X.500 namespace entry can be resolved by an X.500-backed LDAP server even when the host and port are omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The URL can ask for selected attributes and choose whether to search one entry, one level, or a subtree. If parts are missing, the RFC defines defaults for the returned attributes, scope and filter.

sections.title: Authentication and Status
sections.content:
The LDAP URL format has no way to specify credentials. The RFC therefore expects queries made by resolving these URLs to be unauthenticated, with the same security implications as resolving any LDAP query.

The unit metadata records RFC 2255 as the document that later obsoleted RFC 1959.
sections.plainLanguage: An LDAP URL cannot include credentials, so the RFC expects its queries to be unauthenticated. RFC 2255 later replaced this format specification.
